ch08 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: John Huss's introduction frames the franchise as mirroring successive revolutions: Taylor before the ape tribunal recalls Galileo's heresy trial, the Darwinian revolution that toppled humans from evolution's pinnacle is taken to its logical extreme from Boulle's 1963 novel on, and Rise of the Planet of the Apes stages a 'Molecular Revolution' whose wake-up call is addressed to 'human chauvinists' who forget we share the planet with other species. He reads the cover's interspecies erotica through the Sexual Revolution, quoting Elizabeth Anscombe on contraceptive intercourse and asking whether her argument can get us over the species line, and closes with President Morsi's Tahrir Square allegory of the films: 'We are human, we did do this to ourselves.'

chapters.file: ch09 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
ch10 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
ch11 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Kristin Andrews uses Taylor's silent attempts to show Zira he has a mind - mouthing answers, wiggling his fingers when she mentions the Hopkins Manual Dexterity Test - to stage the problem of other minds, pushing against Descartes's claim that language is required for thought and Mill's argument from analogy, while Dr. Zaius can always redescribe it all as 'a definite gift for mimicry.' Drawing on her fieldwork with the orangutan Cecep (the leaf-wiping pantomime, guiding the frightened Aldrin home from the turtle scare), she argues against reducing mindreading to false-belief tasks and for knowing minds through shared interaction, inductive overhypotheses, and natural context. She ends with an extended-mind point - 'when you're in a cage, you act caged,' and we offload thinking onto our homes and tools - so lab studies can show what apes can do but never what they can't.

chapters.file: ch12 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Sara Waller argues the films show language operating as a tyranny that measures minds and withholds moral standing: Dodge mocking signing Caesar as a 'stupid monkey,' Zaius dismissing Taylor's speech as mimicry, 1894 literacy tests used to disenfranchise Black voters, and IQ tests whose vocabulary sections double-count language skill. She surveys the non-linguistic tests the apes face - the Hopkins dexterity test, the Wisconsin Multiphasic, Kohler's banana-and-boxes task ('Because I loathe bananas'), the Lucas Tower, Caesar's cookie-jar deception - and then deploys Quine's 'gavagai' inscrutability of reference to argue that speech cannot be the ultimate measure of intelligence or moral worth. Nova's hand over Taylor's mouth and Zira and Cornelius's 'be clever... be quiet' suggest that under oppression, silence is the smart play.

chapters.file: ch13 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Don Fallis proposes deception rather than language as the personhood test: following Dennett, a deceiver must be a second-order intentional system who can want someone else to have a false belief, as when General Thade lies to Senator Sandar about Ari's kidnapping, Zira and Cornelius feign muteness before the Presidential Commission, and Caesar fakes his own electrocution in Conquest. The roles' reversal makes this a test for the films' mute humans too, while Descartes's beast machines, Wittgenstein on dogs that cannot simulate pain, and Lloyd Morgan's canon voice the skeptical reading of fake alarm calls and Koko's 'Cat did it.' Against them Fallis invokes Occam's Razor over Hare, Call and Tomasello's food-competition experiments: apes track who sees what, but they fail the misinformed false-belief version, so real apes may not be 'sneaky enough to be people.'

chapters.file: ch14 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
ch15 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Bernard Rollin reads Dr. Zaius's tribunal as 'scientific ideology' in action - 'human see, human do' refuses to believe its own eyes, just as bishops refused to look through Galileo's telescope. He traces the ideology from Newton's 'hypotheses non fingo' through logical positivism's verifiability criterion (which validates the Hasslein Curve prediction while rendering 'there are intelligent beings in Heaven' meaningless) and Wittgenstein's point that 'killing is wrong' is not a fact of the universe, to the 'science is value-free' dogma that left animal pain untested and untreated - as he documents from his own campaign: the empty analgesic literature search, the 1985 federal legislation, and the pain physiologist whose dog research refutes his own denial. Zira's neurosurgery on mute humans repeats what Descartes's beast-machine doctrine licensed, and IASP's language requirement for pain collapses into a Cratylus-grade confusion of necessary and sufficient conditions ('You can't step into the same river once').

chapters.file: ch16 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Massimo Pigliucci reads Rise as a Greek tragedy of hubris and asks whether Will Rodman dosing his father with ALZ-112 was wrong, first dissolving the 'it's unnatural' objection and probing the cure/enhancement border with Daniels's Peter-and-Johnny growth-hormone case, vaccination-as-enhancement, and Eubulides's bald-man paradox. He then runs the decision through three ethical theories: Millian consequentialism condemns it by its results (his father dies and humanity goes extinct, though chimp happiness might outweigh that), Kant's humanity formula condemns using his father as an unconsenting experimental subject, and Aristotelian virtue ethics vindicates Will's compassion and courage - Pigliucci's own view, since sometimes our best is just not enough. He closes by rejecting Baylis and Robert's technological-inevitability thesis (we abandoned the Concorde, CFCs, and nuclear weapons before) and lets Jacobs's plunge into San Francisco Bay stand as the penalty for market hubris.

chapters.file: ch17 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
ch18 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Travis Timmerman argues the series dramatizes Singer's equal consideration of interests: Zira frees Taylor once he writes 'My name is Taylor' because like interests must count equally regardless of species, while Dr. Zaius's erasing the writing, lobotomizing Landon, and destroying the cave artifacts is pure speciesism in Bentham's 'Can they suffer?' sense. He rejects the crude 'humans are smarter' argument (it would strip severely cognitively disabled humans of standing) and Nussbaum's species-normal version (it would permit caging Zira and Cornelius since normal apes are mute), then deploys Plato's Euthyphro dilemma against Locke-style God-given rights: a deity bellowing that human interests outrank ape interests is arbitrary unless grounded in independent reasons. Since farming severely cognitively disabled humans is obviously wrong and species membership is morally irrelevant, it is equally wrong to factory-farm and experiment on animals - so, like Caesar in Battle for the Planet of the Apes, become vegetarian.

chapters.file: ch19 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Jonas-Sebastien Beaudry defends a 'moderate speciesism' built on relationships rather than individual capacities: Taylor's trial strips him of clothes, name, and speech - the symbols of ethical community - showing how institutional speciesism rationalizes domination behind the Sacred Scrolls' Declaration-of-Independence-style self-evidence. Against Singer's anti-speciesist challenge that any distinctively human capacity is shared by some animals or missing from some humans, he argues both camps wrongly pedestal intrinsic traits, and reads Taylor's love for the mute Nova together with the failed Project Nim as showing that within-species bonds of love, care, and family are genuinely and justifiably valuable without licensing mistreatment. Bernard Williams's 'The Human Prejudice' - should we surrender to superior invading aliens? - marks where impartial anti-speciesism leads, while Zaius's 'Man is evil' and the doomsday-bomb ending show extreme speciesism as self-fulfilling prophecy.

chapters.file: ch20 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
ch21 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: David Morgan separates the franchise's two kinds of time travel. Forward travel is physically respectable: special-relativistic time dilation (Taylor's six months against nearly 700 Earth years implies 99.99997 percent of light speed) and gravitational dilation near black holes, confirmed daily by muon lifetimes and GPS satellite corrections. Backward travel, as when Cornelius, Zira, and Milo flee the doomsday blast to 1973, invites the Grandfather Paradox - Hasslein killing the apes would erase the future they came from - but the films resolve it through a closed causal loop in which Hasslein's killings set Caesar's rebellion in motion. Morgan then reads the Aldo-versus-Caesar continuity clash between Escape and Conquest through Hasslein's freeway-of-time speech as a multiple-timelines model aligned with the Many Worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics, which also lets fans file the Burton and Rise reboots as parallel-universe futures.

chapters.file: ch22 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Ralph Shain argues forward and backward time travel are categorically different: relativistic time dilation is conceptually harmless (in Boulle's novel Merou could not return to Soror for a thousand years), but Escape from the Planet of the Apes' backward jump is conceptually impossible because it treats the open future as fixed like the past - Hasslein's plan to kill baby Milo is the Grandfather Paradox, checked against presentist, possibilist, and eternalist ontologies of time. The real philosophical engine is Aristotle's sea-battle argument from the law of excluded middle: since Cornelius's story of the takeover is past for the apes and future for 1973 humans, the film's causal loop (Milo saved at the circus) enacts the fatalist conclusion that the ape takeover will necessarily occur. Hasslein's freeway image of time defeats itself - switching lanes means landing in the past of a different, parallel universe, so the apes' jump would be travel between worlds, not times.

chapters.file: ch23 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
ch24 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Greg Littmann maps Ape City onto Plato's Republic class by class: orangutan rulers who legislate, censor, and propagandize; gorilla warriors who enforce; chimpanzee producers who do all the work - including, pointedly, the science Plato made no provision for; and humans as the 'barbarians' Plato says may be enslaved or exterminated. The overlaps are detailed: the Sacred Scrolls' first article of faith functions as the noble lie's myth of the metals, orangutan funerals promise heaven to keep gorillas unafraid of death, and Zaius's erasing of Taylor's dust-writing and blowing up of the archaeological cave enact the rulers' duty to supervise stories. But the films also refute Plato: hereditary orangutans show that power corrupts philosopher kings, Dr. Honorius's 'reason' is dogma serving the faith, the gelding threat that finally breaks Taylor cracks the tripartite-soul analogy of justice, and democracy's rough virtue is that it lets us remove rulers 'without sticking anybody with iron spears.'

chapters.file: ch25 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Leslie Dale Feldman reads the 1968 film's blasted opening as Hobbes's state of nature - 'solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short' - with the Lawgiver's 'Beware the beast Man' scroll echoing Hobbes's three causes of war (competition, fear, glory) and Plato's Ring of Gyges explaining why even the 'just' man acts rightly only under compulsion, both grounding the social contract's origin story. She then casts Dr. Zaius as Alexis de Tocqueville's tyranny of the majority - erasing Taylor's writing, lobotomizing Landon, and sealing Cornelius's cave 'to spare them all the care of thinking' - with Rousseau's man 'born free; and everywhere he is in chains' behind it. The chapter also traces Rod Serling's Twilight Zone fingerprints (nuclear-war twist endings like 'Time Enough at Last,' the cave of 'The Old Man in the Cave,' Adam-and-Eve survivor pairs, the beauty reversals of 'Eye of the Beholder') and reads Taylor and Nova's westward ride through Turner's frontier thesis and Kennedy's New Frontier, holding Serling's Hobbesian pessimism and his hope in tension.

holes.name: The Problem of Other Minds
holes.what: The classic problem of how I can know that anyone besides myself has a mind, since I directly experience only my own.
holes.why: Chapter 11 stages exactly this problem in Zira's struggle to know that Taylor thinks while Dr. Zaius explains everything as 'a gift for mimicry,' but the taxonomy has no slug for it.

holes.name: Mindreading / Theory of Mind (false belief)
holes.what: The capacity to attribute beliefs, desires, and intentions to others, master-tested by false-belief tasks and often taken to ground personhood.
holes.why: Chapter 13 settles whether apes are 'sneaky enough to be people' on whether they can mindread - attribute false beliefs per Hare, Call and Tomasello - and chapter 11's folk-psychology critique of mindreading uses the same concept, which the taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Scientism (Science as Ideology)
holes.what: The dogmatic extension of scientific authority into a quasi-religious worldview that dismisses ethics and consciousness as meaningless or outside science's scope.
holes.why: Chapter 15's whole diagnosis is Rollin's 'scientific ideology' embodied in Dr. Zaius, Minister of Science and Chief Defender of the Faith, and the taxonomy has no scientism slug.

holes.name: Logical Positivism (verifiability principle)
holes.what: The doctrine that a statement is meaningful only if it can in principle be verified (or falsified) by experience, banishing ethics and metaphysics as meaningless.
holes.why: Chapter 15 explains the verifiability criterion and applies it to the Hasslein Curve prediction versus 'there are intelligent beings in Heaven'; the existing 'falsification' slug is Popper's rival doctrine, not positivism.

holes.name: Alexis de Tocqueville
holes.what: French political thinker whose Democracy in America warns that majority opinion becomes a 'tyranny' raising 'formidable barriers around the liberty of opinion.'
holes.why: Chapter 25 interprets Dr. Zaius's censorship, Landon's lobotomy, and 'what remains, but to spare them all the care of thinking?' through Tocqueville's tyranny of the majority, but the taxonomy has no slug for him.
